title: The Journal and the Poem: Alfoxden and Grasmere, 1797–1803
subtitle: Dorothy Wordsworth's journals, William Wordsworth's poems and Coleridge's notebooks — Somerset, Germany, the Lake District and Calais, 1797–1803
intro: In July 1797 William Wordsworth and his sister Dorothy took a big, half-furnished house called Alfoxden at the foot of the Quantock Hills in Somerset, three miles from the cottage at Nether Stowey where Samuel Taylor Coleridge lived. For the next year the three of them walked almost daily, by day and by moonlight, and out of those walks came Lyrical Ballads (1798), the book usually taken as the opening of English Romantic poetry. In January 1798 Dorothy began a small journal of weather, light, moon and the people met on the road. After a winter in Germany the Wordsworths settled in December 1799 at a former inn at Town End, Grasmere — the house later called Dove Cottage — and in May 1800 Dorothy began the Grasmere journal, which runs, with a lost notebook for most of 1801, to January 1803.

This chapter lays those journals beside the poems that grew from them. Dorothy met an old leech-gatherer on the road in October 1800; William's 'Resolution and Independence' came eighteen months later, and Dorothy copied it out again and again as he revised it. She saw the daffodils by Ullswater on 15 April 1802; 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' was written two years later. She watched London from Westminster Bridge on the morning of 31 July 1802 from the roof of the Dover coach; William's sonnet on the same view was later printed with a wrong date. The journal is not a draft of the poems, and the poems are not copies of the journal: the reader can see where the two lean on each other and where they part.

Around the two of them stand other eyes. Coleridge's letters and notebooks run alongside — the November 1797 walk on which the Ancient Mariner was planned, the Keswick years, the verse letter to Sara Hutchinson of 4 April 1802 that became 'Dejection: An Ode'. A Home Office agent, James Walsh, was sent to watch the 'nest of democrats' at Alfoxden in August 1797, and his reports survive. Charles Lamb argued with the poems by post; Robert Southey reviewed the first edition coldly; their Bristol publisher Joseph Cottle and the young William Hazlitt left memoirs of visits to Alfoxden written decades later. John Wordsworth, the sea-captain brother, wrote to Mary Hutchinson about the second edition before his ship was lost in 1805. Annette Vallon, the Frenchwoman who bore William's daughter Caroline in 1792, is present through letters of 1793 that never reached him, and through the August 1802 visit to Calais.

Much of the record here is letters and later recollection rather than diary, and the chapter says so entry by entry. Dorothy's journals themselves are not tidy: she often wrote up several days at once and misdated entries, one notebook is lost, and lines in the entry about William's wedding to Mary Hutchinson on 4 October 1802 were later struck through by an unknown hand. Mary and Sara Hutchinson appear mostly through what others wrote to and about them, because few of their own letters from these years survive.

The convergences are the shared days: the walk of 13 November 1797; the evening of 23 March 1798 when Coleridge brought the finished Mariner; the October 1800 week when Christabel was dropped from the second edition; April 1802, when the 'Dejection' letter, the daffodils and Coleridge's recital fall within three weeks; early August 1802, with Dorothy and William on the Calais sands and Coleridge alone on Scafell; and 4 October 1802, when William married, Dorothy stayed behind at the house, and 'Dejection' appeared in a London newspaper.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Dorothy Wordsworth often wrote entries in batches and sometimes gave the wrong day of the month; where her weekday and date disagree, editors (Knight 1897, de Selincourt, Moorman, Woof) have corrected them, and the dates here follow the corrected readings. Some of Coleridge's and Wordsworth's letters are undated in manuscript and dated by editors; these are marked approx.

eyes.name: Dorothy Wordsworth
eyes.role: Aged 26–31; William's sister and housekeeper, walking companion, copyist of his manuscripts
eyes.where: Alfoxden, Somerset (1797–98); Goslar (1798–99); Dove Cottage, Grasmere (from Dec 1799)
eyes.authenticity: The Alfoxden journal survives only in transcript (the manuscript is lost); the four surviving Grasmere notebooks are at the Wordsworth Trust (DCMS 19, 20, 25, 31); a fifth, covering most of 1801, is missing. William Knight's 1897 edition omitted and smoothed passages; later editions (de Selincourt 1941, Moorman 1971, Woof 1991) restore them. Some lines in the wedding entry are struck through by an unidentified hand.
eyes.bio: Orphaned young and separated from William for years, Dorothy set up house with him in 1795 and stayed with him for the rest of her life. Her journals record weather, light, plants, the poor on the roads, and the daily making of William's poems — which she copied, read aloud and sometimes supplied the raw material for. She is the closest observer in this chapter and the one whose words most often reappear in someone else's verse.

sources.title: Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth, ed. William Knight, vol. 1 (1897), Project Gutenberg
Diplomatic transcription of the first Grasmere Journal notebook (DCMS 20), Romantic Circles
Two pages from the Grasmere Journal (Wordsworth Trust DCMS 19 and 31)

eyes.name: William Wordsworth
eyes.role: Aged 27–32; poet with a small legacy and no profession; father of a daughter in France
eyes.where: Alfoxden; Goslar; Grasmere; London and Calais in summer 1802
eyes.vantage_label: the poet whose poems the journals feed
eyes.form: dated poems and manuscripts, dated letters; later dictated notes (Fenwick notes, 1843)
eyes.authenticity: Letters edited by de Selincourt, revised by Shaver and Moorman (The Early Years, 1967). Many poem titles carry dates added years later, some wrong (the Westminster Bridge sonnet was printed as 'Sept. 3, 1803'). The Fenwick notes are recollections dictated in old age and are flagged as such.
eyes.bio: Wordsworth had lived in revolutionary France in 1791–92, where Annette Vallon bore his daughter. Back in England, short of money and politically suspect, he found in Somerset and then Grasmere the routine that produced Lyrical Ballads, the early Prelude and the 1807 Poems in Two Volumes. The journal entries here show the poems in their working state — begun, recited, copied, abandoned, finished.

sources.title: The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, ed. Knight, vol. 2, Project Gutenberg
Lyrical Ballads: an electronic scholarly edition (Texas A&M)

eyes.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
eyes.role: Aged 25–30; poet, lecturer, journalist; supported from 1798 by a Wedgwood annuity
eyes.where: Nether Stowey (1797–98); Germany (1798–99); Greta Hall, Keswick (from July 1800)
eyes.form: notebooks and dated letters; later recollections (Biographia Literaria, 1817)
eyes.authenticity: Notebooks edited by Kathleen Coburn (from 1957); letters by E. L. Griggs (1956–71) and earlier by E. H. Coleridge (1895). The 4 April 1802 verse letter to Sara Hutchinson survives in copies; the shortened 'Dejection: An Ode' was printed in the Morning Post on 4 October 1802. Biographia Literaria (1817) recalls the Lyrical Ballads plan and the spy story at twenty years' distance.
eyes.bio: Coleridge drew the Wordsworths to Somerset and talked Lyrical Ballads into being; the Ancient Mariner opened it. In the Lakes from 1800 he was ill, increasingly dependent on opium, unhappily married and in love with Mary Hutchinson's sister Sara. His comings and goings punctuate Dorothy's journal, and his own writing of these years measures the distance between his state and the Wordsworths' household.

sources.title: Letters of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, ed. E. H. Coleridge (1895), vol. 1, Internet Archive

eyes.name: James Walsh
eyes.role: Home Office agent, sent from London in August 1797
eyes.side: the British government (Home Office, under the Duke of Portland)
eyes.authenticity: Walsh's reports and the letter of the Bath physician Dr Daniel Lysons that prompted them are in the Home Office papers at The National Archives (HO 42 series); they were first published by A. J. Eagleston in 1934. The 'Spy Nozy' anecdote (the spy overhearing talk of Spinoza) comes from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria (1817), not from Walsh's reports.
eyes.bio: Walsh was an experienced agent who had already followed the radical lecturer John Thelwall. Reports that strangers at Alfoxden walked by night, carried a camp-stool and took notes of the brook reached the Home Office in a wartime invasion scare. His reports are the outside view of the poets: politics, not poetry.

sources.title: The National Archives: Adam Nicolson on the Somerset year and the Home Office surveillance

eyes.name: Thomas Poole
eyes.role: Aged 32; prosperous tanner of Nether Stowey, radical sympathiser, Coleridge's patron
eyes.vantage_label: the neighbour who made the arrangements
eyes.form: dated letters (largely as printed in M. E. Sandford, Thomas Poole and his Friends, 1888)
eyes.authenticity: Poole's papers were used by his relative Mrs Henry Sandford for her 1888 book; many survive in the British Library. Entries here rely on the letters as printed and on standard biographies; exact days are marked approx.
eyes.bio: Poole found Coleridge his cottage in 1796 and helped the Wordsworths take Alfoxden in 1797, standing as their local guarantor. When the landlord's family refused to renew the lease after the spy scare, it was Poole's standing in the village that had been spent. He stayed Coleridge's most loyal correspondent while Coleridge was in Germany.

eyes.name: Joseph Cottle
eyes.role: Aged 27–28; Bristol bookseller and minor poet, first publisher of Lyrical Ballads
eyes.authenticity: Cottle wrote forty years after the events and is known to have misdated letters and reshaped anecdotes; his memoirs are used here only for what he saw and did, with dates approx.
eyes.bio: Cottle had published Coleridge's and Southey's early poems and paid Wordsworth thirty guineas for the copyright of Lyrical Ballads. Before the book appeared he sold the edition to the London firm of J. & A. Arch. His recollection of a visit to Alfoxden is the only account by the man who carried the manuscript to press.

eyes.name: William Hazlitt
eyes.role: Aged 19–20; son of a Unitarian minister at Wem, Shropshire, not yet a writer
eyes.where: Wem and Shrewsbury (Jan 1798); Nether Stowey and Alfoxden (spring 1798)
eyes.form: memoir (written later): 'My First Acquaintance with Poets', The Liberal, 1823
eyes.authenticity: A vivid essay written in 1823 after Hazlitt had quarrelled with both poets; its details (dress, accent, readings) are generally accepted but the day-dates are not given and are approx.
eyes.bio: Hazlitt walked ten miles through mud to hear Coleridge preach at Shrewsbury and was invited to Stowey. He saw Lyrical Ballads in manuscript before publication and heard both poets read aloud. His essay is the best outside picture of the Alfoxden year — written by a man who later turned against them politically.

eyes.name: Charles Lamb
eyes.role: Aged 22–27; clerk at the East India House, London; Coleridge's school friend
eyes.authenticity: Letters edited by Talfourd, Ainger, E. V. Lucas and Marrs; the Gutenberg selection follows the older editions, whose dates for some 1801 letters are editorial.
eyes.bio: Lamb loved Coleridge and the city in equal measure and refused to be converted to mountains. His letters defend the Ancient Mariner against Southey, needle Wordsworth about the second edition, and report the reaction of the poets to his candour. He is the most independent reader in the chapter.

sources.title: The Best Letters of Charles Lamb, Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Robert Southey
eyes.role: Aged 24–29; poet and reviewer; Coleridge's brother-in-law
eyes.side: Bristol and London literary world; from 1803 Keswick
eyes.where: Westbury near Bristol (1798); Greta Hall, Keswick (from 1803)
eyes.vantage_label: reviewer and in-law at a distance
eyes.form: anonymous review (Critical Review, Oct 1798) and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: The Critical Review notice was unsigned but Southey's authorship was known to the circle at once and is not disputed.
eyes.bio: Southey and Coleridge had planned Pantisocracy together and married the Fricker sisters; by 1798 they had quarrelled. His review of Lyrical Ballads was the most damaging early notice, and it hurt because it came from inside the family. In 1803 he moved into Greta Hall and stayed for forty years, long after Coleridge had gone.

sources.title: Lyrical Ballads electronic edition: editor's introduction on reviews

eyes.name: John Wordsworth
eyes.role: Aged 27–32; East India Company officer, from 1801 captain of the Earl of Abergavenny
eyes.where: Dove Cottage (Jan–Sept 1800); London and at sea
eyes.authenticity: Edited by Carl H. Ketcham, The Letters of John Wordsworth (1969); some dates editorial.
eyes.bio: John spent most of 1800 at Dove Cottage and hoped to make the family's fortune on the China voyages. His letters to Mary Hutchinson and William show a plain-spoken reader of Lyrical Ballads. His drowning in February 1805 closed the Grasmere years in grief.

sources.title: Article on John Wordsworth's 1801 letters and the Stoddart review (ARIEL)

eyes.name: Marie-Anne (Annette) Vallon
eyes.role: Aged 26–36; mother of William's daughter Caroline (born Orléans, 15 Dec 1792); royalist sympathiser
eyes.vantage_label: across the Channel, cut off by war
eyes.authenticity: Two letters of March 1793, to William and to Dorothy, were stopped in wartime and found in the archives at Blois; published by G. M. Harper (1916) and Émile Legouis, William Wordsworth and Annette Vallon (1922). Her side of the 1802 visit is not recorded.
eyes.bio: War between Britain and France from February 1793 kept William from Annette and their daughter for nine years. Her letters show a woman pleading for news and imagining a family life that did not come. The Peace of Amiens in 1802 allowed the meeting at Calais that settled matters before William married.

eyes.name: Thomas De Quincey
eyes.role: Aged 17–22; runaway schoolboy, then Oxford student and admirer of Lyrical Ballads
eyes.form: dated letter (1803) and memoir (written later): 'Recollections of the Lake Poets', Tait's Magazine, 1834–40
eyes.authenticity: His 1803 letter to Wordsworth survives at the Wordsworth Trust. The recollections were written thirty years on, after a quarrel, and are flagged as later and partial.
eyes.bio: De Quincey read Lyrical Ballads as a schoolboy and in May 1803 wrote Wordsworth the first fan letter he received. He reached Dove Cottage in 1807 and later took the house over. His portraits of Dorothy in old-age memoir are the most quoted outside view of her, and among the least reliable.

entries.headline: Letters to William and Dorothy that never arrive
entries.digest: Three months after Caroline's birth Annette wrote to William and to his sister, whom she had never met, in a France now at war with Britain. She described the baby, begged for letters, and wrote as though a marriage were only delayed. The letters were stopped in transit and stayed in the departmental archives at Blois for over a century.
entries.source_note: Legouis, William Wordsworth and Annette Vallon (1922); G. M. Harper, Wordsworth's French Daughter (1921). Day as given by Legouis; not checked against the archive here.

entries.headline: A London clerk's week in Coleridge's garden
entries.digest: Lamb took a short holiday from the East India House to stay with Coleridge at Stowey just as the Wordsworths arrived. Coleridge, his foot scalded, stayed behind while the others walked, and wrote the poem later called 'This Lime-Tree Bower my Prison' with Lamb in it. Lamb's later letters show he went home loving the friends and unconverted by the hills.
entries.source_note: Coleridge to Southey, July 1797 (Letters, ed. E. H. Coleridge); Lamb's letters of summer 1797 to Coleridge.

entries.headline: Poole arranges a year's lease of Alfoxden
entries.digest: Poole helped the Wordsworths take Alfoxden House, furnished, for a year at a low rent, and stood as their local reference with the St Albyn family who owned it. The house was three miles from Coleridge's cottage over the Quantocks. Within weeks, gossip about the new tenants was circulating among servants and neighbours.
entries.source_note: Sandford, Thomas Poole and his Friends (1888); standard biographies. Exact date of the agreement not verified here.

entries.headline: The agent arrives to watch the 'emigrants' at Alfoxden
entries.digest: Sent by the Home Office after a Bath doctor reported suspicious strangers, Walsh traced the reported Frenchmen to Alfoxden and lodged in Stowey. He reported that the household was connected with Thelwall, the radical lecturer, who had recently visited, and that the group met with Poole, a known democrat. Local reports of the strangers taking notes and sketches along the brook had been read in London as possible surveying for an invasion.
entries.source_note: Home Office papers, The National Archives (HO 42 series), as published by A. J. Eagleston (1934) and discussed by Holmes and Nicolson; day of report approx.

entries.headline: Not French spies, he concludes, but English radicals
entries.digest: Walsh's follow-up report told London that the strangers were not French agents at all but English sympathisers with reform. No action followed from the Home Office. But the talk in the village did its damage: the Alfoxden lease was not renewed beyond midsummer 1798.
entries.source_note: As above; the reports were first printed in 1934, so no wording is quoted here.

entries.headline: The Ancient Mariner begun as his half of a plan
entries.digest: Coleridge began the long ballad soon after the walk. In Biographia Literaria twenty years later he described the scheme of the joint book: he would make the supernatural feel real, and Wordsworth would make the everyday feel new. The tidy division was written after the event, but it still frames how Lyrical Ballads is read.
entries.source_note: Biographia Literaria (1817), ch. 14; Coleridge's own dating of the Mariner to Nov 1797–Mar 1798.

entries.date_display: Monday 13 November 1797 (walk), described in a letter of c. 20 November
entries.place: The Quantocks toward Watchet and Lynton
entries.headline: Setting out at dusk; a ballad planned on the road
entries.digest: Dorothy, William and Coleridge left Alfoxden late in the afternoon for a walking tour along the Somerset and Devon coast, partly to pay for it by a poem sold to a magazine. Writing to Mary Hutchinson a week later, Dorothy reported that the two men spent the first dark miles working out a ballad together. The ballad outgrew the plan, and the partnership did not survive the composition: Coleridge wrote it alone.
entries.quote: laying the plan of a ballad
entries.source_note: DW to Mary Hutchinson, [20] Nov 1797, in The Early Letters of William and Dorothy Wordsworth (de Selincourt, 1935).

entries.headline: Old Wordsworth remembers suggesting the albatross
entries.digest: In a note dictated to Isabella Fenwick nearly fifty years later, Wordsworth recalled that on this walk he proposed the killing of an albatross and the navigation of the ship by the dead men, having read of albatrosses in Shelvocke's voyage. He said he soon withdrew from the joint work because their manners did not fit. It is a late memory, cherished but not contemporary.
entries.source_note: Fenwick note to 'We are Seven' (1843), in Poetical Works ed. Knight.

entries.headline: A student walks ten miles to hear Coleridge preach
entries.digest: Coleridge was in Shropshire as a candidate for a Unitarian pulpit, the job the Wedgwood annuity would soon free him from. Hazlitt walked through winter mud from Wem to hear him and remembered the sermon as a revelation. A few days later Coleridge invited him to Stowey.
entries.quote: And he went up into the mountain to pray, HIMSELF, ALONE.
entries.source_note: Hazlitt, 'My First Acquaintance with Poets', The Liberal (1823); the sermon text as quoted there.

entries.headline: The Alfoxden journal opens on a wet green hillside
entries.digest: Dorothy's first surviving entry notes the green paths running with water, the young wheat, and the mosses and lichens of winter. The journal is spare and outward-looking, with almost no comment on herself. Moon, stars and light dominate the next weeks; William took phrases from these pages into poems of the same spring.
entries.quote: The green paths down the hill-sides are channels for streams.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight (1897), vol. 1, Alfoxden journal, 20 Jan 1798 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: Asking Cottle to send Erasmus Darwin's Zoonomia
entries.digest: Wordsworth wrote to Cottle in Bristol asking him to send Erasmus Darwin's medical treatise Zoonomia without delay. He used a case in it — a labourer who believed himself cursed with cold by an old woman — for 'Goody Blake and Harry Gill', one of the ballads of that spring. Science and folk belief went into the book side by side.
entries.source_note: WW to Joseph Cottle, [early March 1798], Early Years letters; source of 'Goody Blake' acknowledged in the 1798 Advertisement.

entries.headline: A stunted thorn after the hailstorm
entries.digest: Dorothy walked the hilltops in cold weather and recorded that William wrote some lines on a stunted thorn seen in the storm. The poem became 'The Thorn', one of the most mocked pieces of the 1798 volume. Her entry gives the plain tree before the story was hung on it.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, Alfoxden journal, 19 Mar 1798.

entries.headline: Coleridge brings the finished Ancient Mariner
entries.digest: Coleridge came to dine and brought his ballad, finished. Dorothy recorded it in a single plain sentence and turned to the evening walk under the stars and a horned moon. The poem that opens Lyrical Ballads arrives in her journal as an item of the day.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, Alfoxden journal, 23 Mar 1798.

entries.headline: The publisher's visit: terms agreed, dinner on the grass
entries.digest: Cottle rode out to Alfoxden to settle the publication of the poems and later told a comic story of an Alfoxden picnic that went wrong. He paid thirty guineas for Wordsworth's share and agreed to print the poems anonymously in one volume. His recollections, written forty years later, dramatise himself.
entries.source_note: Cottle, Early Recollections (1837), vol. 1; dates in Cottle are unreliable.

entries.headline: Hearing the ballads before they were printed
entries.digest: Hazlitt spent three weeks around Stowey. At Alfoxden Dorothy kept house while William was away in Bristol, and Hazlitt slept a night there and read the ballads in manuscript. When Wordsworth returned he read Peter Bell aloud outdoors; Coleridge chanted his own verse. Hazlitt remembered Wordsworth's northern burr and Coleridge calling his friend too matter-of-fact.
entries.source_note: Hazlitt, 'My First Acquaintance with Poets' (1823).

entries.headline: The three cross to Germany
entries.digest: Coleridge, his friend John Chester and the Wordsworths sailed from Yarmouth for Hamburg; Coleridge's later account makes comedy of the passengers, while Dorothy was miserably seasick. In Germany they parted: Coleridge to Ratzeburg and Göttingen to study, the Wordsworths to a cold winter in Goslar. Lyrical Ballads came out in London about a fortnight after they landed.
entries.source_note: Coleridge, 'Satyrane's Letters' (The Friend, 1809; Biographia 1817); Dorothy's Hamburg journal (Sept 1798).

entries.headline: The family reviewer is unimpressed
entries.digest: Southey's unsigned notice in the Critical Review dismissed most of the ballads and called the Ancient Mariner a failure of taste and sense, singling out 'The Idiot Boy' and 'The Thorn' as wasted effort. He praised 'Tintern Abbey'. Coleridge and Wordsworth knew who had written it.
entries.quote: a Dutch attempt at German sublimity
entries.source_note: Critical Review, 2nd ser., 24 (Oct 1798); see TAMU editor's introduction.

entries.headline: Lamb defends the Mariner to Southey's face
entries.digest: Writing to Southey, Lamb challenged the review directly: the Ancient Mariner had moved him as few things had, whatever its faults. He praised the strangeness of the voyage and the mariner's isolation. It is the first recorded reader's defence of the poem.
entries.quote: a right English attempt, and a successful one
entries.source_note: Lamb to Southey, 8 Nov 1798 (Best Letters of Charles Lamb, Gutenberg, letter XVI).

entries.headline: Snowbound in Goslar, writing about childhood
entries.digest: Cut off by the language and the coldest winter of the century, Wordsworth wrote the 'Lucy' poems and the first passages about his own boyhood that would grow into The Prelude, sending some in letters to Coleridge. Dorothy copied them. The German winter turned him toward the Lake District he had grown up in.
entries.source_note: WW and DW letters to Coleridge, Dec 1798 (Early Years); manuscript JJ of the Prelude.

entries.headline: Breaking news of a dead child to Coleridge abroad
entries.digest: Coleridge's infant son Berkeley died in February 1799 after smallpox inoculation. Poole, who was looking after Sara Coleridge's affairs, advised delaying the news so as not to unsettle Coleridge's studies, and wrote himself when it could be delayed no longer. Coleridge's letters of April 1799 from Göttingen record the blow and his decision to stay on.
entries.source_note: Poole's letters as printed in Sandford (1888); STC to Poole, April 1799 (Letters, ed. E. H. Coleridge).

entries.headline: Meeting Sara Hutchinson; touring the Lakes with Wordsworth
entries.digest: Coleridge joined the Wordsworths at the Hutchinson farm at Sockburn and there met Mary's sister Sara, whose hand he recorded holding by the fire in his notebook. He and Wordsworth then toured the Lakes, and he wrote to Dorothy that William was thinking of a house at Grasmere. The notebook begins the long, unhappy love that runs through the next years.
entries.source_note: Coleridge, Notebooks ed. Coburn, vol. 1 (entries of Nov 1799).

entries.headline: Arriving at the cottage after a winter walk
entries.digest: William and Dorothy reached the former inn at Town End after walking and riding across the Pennines in snow, a journey he described to Coleridge in a long letter a few days later. The house was small, cold and damp. It was their first home of their own in the Lakes, and they would stay eight years.
entries.source_note: WW to STC, 24 and 27 Dec 1799 (Early Years).

entries.headline: Left alone, she begins a journal to please William
entries.digest: William and John set out for Yorkshire and Dorothy walked part of the way with them, then sat on a stone and cried. She began the Grasmere journal, she wrote, because she would not quarrel with herself and because it would give William pleasure on his return. Within days it was full of flowers, weather and passing beggars.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, Grasmere journal, 14 May 1800.

entries.headline: A tall beggar woman and her two lying boys
entries.digest: A tall woman in a cloak came to the door with a baby and Dorothy gave her food; later she met two boys chasing a butterfly who claimed their mother was dead. She recorded both meetings in detail, including the boys' cheerful lie. William used the entry for 'Beggars' in March 1802, working directly from her pages.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 10 June 1800; the 1802 use recorded in the journal for 13 Mar 1802.

entries.headline: Explaining away Christabel's exclusion
entries.digest: In letters to friends such as Humphry Davy, Coleridge said that Christabel was too long and too unlike the other poems, and that it would be printed separately. He continued to praise Wordsworth extravagantly. Notebooks of the same months show illness and self-reproach.
entries.source_note: STC letters of Oct 1800 (Letters ed. Griggs, vol. 1).

entries.headline: The old leech-gatherer on the road
entries.digest: Dorothy and William met an old man bent almost double who had once been hurt by a cart and now lived by gathering leeches, which were getting scarce. She wrote down his history, his Scottish birth and his poverty with exact details of prices. Eighteen months later this entry became 'Resolution and Independence'.
entries.quote: leeches were formerly 2s. 6d. per 100; they are now 30s.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 3 Oct 1800.

entries.headline: Christabel will not go in the book
entries.digest: After Coleridge had read Christabel aloud to great delight on the 4th and 5th, the household decided not to print it in the second volume of Lyrical Ballads. Dorothy records the decision without comment. Coleridge walked back to Keswick the next day; the poem remained unpublished until 1816.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 4–7 Oct 1800.

entries.headline: A frank reader of the second edition
entries.digest: Sent the new two-volume Lyrical Ballads (dated 1800, issued in January 1801), Lamb wrote to Wordsworth that some poems pleased him greatly — the Lucy song among them — but objected that some poems pointed their moral too openly. He also defended the Ancient Mariner against Wordsworth's own disparaging note on it.
entries.source_note: Lamb to Wordsworth, Jan 1801 (Best Letters, letter XXXIV); date editorial.

entries.headline: A sailor's verdict on a too-friendly review
entries.digest: John wrote to William that a review of the second edition by their friend John Stoddart was too much of a panegyric and that readers would see it was written by a friend. In another letter he admitted he had been disappointed by 'Michael' at first and then delighted.
entries.source_note: John Wordsworth to WW, 28 Jan 1801 (Letters of John Wordsworth, ed. Ketcham, 1969), as discussed in ARIEL article.

entries.headline: Declining the mountains: a hymn to London
entries.digest: Answering an invitation to the Lakes, Lamb listed what he loved in the city — the Strand, the shops, the crowds, the theatres, the night streets — and said mountains could not compete. It was an answer to the creed of the Preface as much as to the invitation.
entries.quote: I have passed all my days in London
entries.source_note: Lamb to Wordsworth, 30 Jan 1801 (Best Letters, letter XXXV).

entries.headline: The poets bite back at his criticism
entries.digest: Lamb told Thomas Manning that Wordsworth had replied to his criticisms with a long lecture on what the poems were meant to do, and that Coleridge had followed with a letter of his own. He was amused and a little bruised. The exchange shows how hard the household defended the book.
entries.quote: All the North of England are in a turmoil.
entries.source_note: Lamb to Manning, 15 Feb 1801 (Best Letters, letter XXXVII).

entries.place: White Moss, between Grasmere and Rydal
entries.headline: An old sailor begging on the moss
entries.digest: Walking with William, Dorothy met an old man who had been at sea and now begged, and wrote down his talk and appearance. Entries like this in the winter of 1801–02 are crowded with beggars, discharged soldiers and sailors, widows on the road — the human cost of war and enclosure seen from a cottage door.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 22 Dec 1801.

entries.headline: A verse letter to Sara Hutchinson
entries.digest: Coleridge wrote a long, private poem addressed to Sara, lamenting his unhappy marriage, his failing health and the loss of his power to feel the beauty he could still see. It was not meant for print. Cut, re-addressed and made impersonal, it became 'Dejection: An Ode'.
entries.source_note: Verse letter to Sara Hutchinson, 4 April 1802 (Dove Cottage MS copies); Coleridge, Poetical Works ed. E. H. Coleridge (1912).

entries.headline: Daffodils by the lake in the wind
entries.digest: Walking back to Grasmere along Ullswater in a strong wind, Dorothy and William came on a long belt of daffodils by the shore. She wrote that some rested their heads on stones as on pillows and the rest seemed to laugh and dance with the wind. William's poem on them was written two years later and drew on this entry.
entries.quote: I never saw daffodils so beautiful.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 15 Apr 1802; manuscript DCMS 19 (Wordsworth Trust).

entries.headline: Coleridge recites the verses to Sara
entries.digest: Coleridge, who had arrived unexpectedly the day before, repeated the verses he had written to Sara. Dorothy recorded that she was affected by them and was in miserable spirits afterwards. William had been answering Coleridge's moods in poems of his own that same spring.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 20–21 Apr 1802.

entries.headline: Writing out 'The Leech Gatherer' the morning after
entries.digest: William had begun the poem the night before, and Dorothy copied it out for him. Over the next days she records him working at it almost without stopping, tiring himself, and making changes. Her 1800 entry and her 1802 copies bracket the poem's making.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 3–9 May 1802.

entries.headline: Defending the old man against Sara's criticism
entries.digest: Sara Hutchinson had written that the leech-gatherer poem was dull. William replied at length, explaining that the old man's firmness of mind, met by a young man in despair, was the whole point, and that she should read it as he felt it. Dorothy added a sharper postscript. He nonetheless revised the poem heavily.
entries.source_note: WW and DW to Mary and Sara Hutchinson, 14 June 1802 (Early Years).

entries.headline: The leech-gatherer poem finished
entries.digest: Dorothy recorded that William finished 'The Leech Gatherer' that day, and the next day she copied it out for Coleridge and for themselves. They were about to leave for Yorkshire, London and France. The finished poem, later 'Resolution and Independence', had changed much since the May version.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 4–5 July 1802.

entries.headline: London at dawn from the roof of the Dover coach
entries.digest: Dorothy and William left London early on the Dover coach from Charing Cross. Crossing Westminster Bridge she saw the city, St Paul's, the river and its boats clear in the morning light without the usual smoke, and wrote that it had something like the purity of one of nature's own sights. The same view became William's sonnet.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, 31 July 1802.

entries.headline: A sonnet on the sleeping city
entries.digest: William composed a sonnet on the morning view from the bridge. When it was printed in Poems in Two Volumes (1807) its title carried the date 3 September 1803; later editions changed the year to 1802 but kept September — a slip that shows how unreliable the poems' own dates can be against the journal.
entries.quote: Earth has not anything to show more fair
entries.source_note: Poems in Two Volumes (1807); Dorothy's journal entry of 31 July 1802 fixes the day.

entries.headline: Sonnets on the beach and on Napoleon's France
entries.digest: At Calais William wrote a run of sonnets: on the evening sea with his daughter walking beside him, on the crowds acclaiming Bonaparte as First Consul, on England seen across the strait. They are the poems of a man settling an old life before starting a new one.
entries.source_note: Poems in Two Volumes (1807), 'Sonnets dedicated to Liberty'; dates from titles ('Calais, August 1802').

entries.headline: Finding Annette and Caroline
entries.digest: After a night crossing the Wordsworths found Annette and her nine-year-old daughter at a lodging in Calais and stayed four weeks. Dorothy's account, written up later, is mostly about the evening walks on the sands, the light on the water and the child, and very little about what was said between the adults.
entries.quote: We found out Annette and C. chez Madame Avril
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight, entry for 31 July–1 Aug 1802.

entries.headline: Alone on Scafell, writing to Sara
entries.digest: While the Wordsworths were in Calais, Coleridge went walking alone across the western fells and wrote a running letter to Sara Hutchinson. From the top of Scafell he described the view and then a descent down ledges he could not climb back up, lying on his back and laughing. It is often cited as the first recorded rock climb in England.
entries.source_note: STC to Sara Hutchinson, 1–9 Aug 1802 (Letters ed. Griggs, vol. 2).

entries.place: Gallow Hill and Brompton church, Yorkshire
entries.headline: William marries Mary Hutchinson; Dorothy stays at the house
entries.digest: Dorothy wrote the wedding entry later. She had worn the wedding ring overnight and gave it to William that morning, and he blessed her; she did not go to the church but lay on her bed until told the party was coming back, then went out to meet her brother and his wife. Some lines of the passage were later struck through by an unknown hand. The three set off for Grasmere the same day.
entries.source_note: Grasmere journal, 4 Oct 1802 (DCMS 31; text in Woof, The Grasmere Journals, 1991; omitted in part by Knight).

entries.headline: 'Dejection: An Ode' appears on the wedding day
entries.digest: Coleridge's ode, shorn of Sara's name and of the private lament, appeared in the Morning Post on William's wedding day, which was also the seventh anniversary of Coleridge's own marriage. The coincidence of dates has been read as deliberate; Coleridge did not explain it.
entries.source_note: Morning Post, 4 Oct 1802.

entries.headline: The Grasmere journal breaks off
entries.digest: With Mary now in the house, the journal thinned and stopped in mid-January 1803, its last entries about firelight, reading, and small purchases. Dorothy later kept travel journals (Scotland, 1803) but never again a daily journal of the same kind for these years.
entries.source_note: Journals ed. Knight; Woof (1991) on the final entries.

entries.headline: A seventeen-year-old's letter to the poet
entries.digest: De Quincey wrote Wordsworth a long, anxious letter of homage, saying Lyrical Ballads had meant more to him than any other book and asking for his friendship. Wordsworth answered kindly in July. It was the first sign the book had found its own readers among the young.
entries.source_note: De Quincey to WW, 31 May 1803 (Wordsworth Trust); reply WW to De Quincey, 29 July 1803 (Early Years).

entries.headline: The reviewer moves into Coleridge's house
entries.digest: After the death of his baby daughter, Southey and his wife came to Greta Hall to stay with the Coleridges. He stayed for the rest of his life, eventually supporting Coleridge's family as well as his own. The house that had been Coleridge's base became Southey's.
entries.source_note: Southey's letters, 1803 (New Letters, ed. Curry).

entries.headline: Coda: John's ship lost off Portland
entries.digest: On 5 February 1805 the Earl of Abergavenny, under John Wordsworth's command, struck the Shambles off Portland Bill and sank; John was among the many drowned. William's letters to Sir George Beaumont and others that month show grief and a struggle to find meaning in it. Dorothy wrote that she could not write. The Grasmere years were over.
entries.source_note: WW to Sir George Beaumont, Feb 1805 (Early Years); wreck of 5 Feb 1805 widely recorded.

entries.headline: First sight of Dorothy — remembered thirty years later
entries.digest: De Quincey finally reached Grasmere in late 1807 and later described the Wordsworth household in Tait's Magazine. His portrait of Dorothy's quick, restless manner and sunburnt face is much quoted, but it was written after a quarrel and shaped by hindsight.
entries.source_note: De Quincey, 'Recollections of the Lake Poets', Tait's Edinburgh Magazine (1834–40).

claims.claim: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner planned on a walk; Coleridge begins it alone
claims.evidence: DW to Mary Hutchinson, Nov 1797; Biographia Literaria ch. 14; Fenwick note (1843)

claims.claim: Writes lines on a stunted thorn — the start of 'The Thorn'
Brings the finished Ancient Mariner to Alfoxden
Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems, anonymous, appears in London under the J. & A. Arch imprint (sheets printed by Cottle's Bristol printer)
Southey's hostile review in the Critical Review
Decision not to print Christabel in the second volume
Second edition, two volumes, with the Preface and Wordsworth's name, published by Longman
claims.evidence: TAMU introduction; Lamb's and John Wordsworth's letters of Jan 1801

claims.claim: 'Beggars' written from Dorothy's entry of 10 June 1800
Verse letter to Sara Hutchinson — the source of 'Dejection'
Begins 'The Leech Gatherer' from Dorothy's 1800 entry
Finishes 'The Leech Gatherer' (later 'Resolution and Independence') after revision prompted by Sara Hutchinson
claims.evidence: Grasmere journal, 4 July 1802; WW letter of 14 June 1802

claims.claim: Westminster Bridge sonnet composed (later printed with a wrong date)
claims.evidence: Grasmere journal, 31 July 1802; Poems in Two Volumes (1807)

claims.claim: 'Dejection: An Ode' published in the Morning Post
'I wandered lonely as a cloud' written, two years after the 15 April 1802 entry
Poems in Two Volumes prints the daffodils, Westminster Bridge, Calais and leech-gatherer poems

convergences.label: The spy at Stowey
convergences.note: Walsh saw a political cell; Poole was the local democrat whose name kept recurring in the reports; Coleridge turned the episode into a comic anecdote in 1817. The real cost — the lost lease — fell on the Wordsworths.

convergences.label: The walk on which the Ancient Mariner was planned
convergences.note: Dorothy's letter, written a week later, is the only contemporary record; Wordsworth's albatross and Coleridge's division of labour are both remembered decades on, and each memory flatters its teller a little.

convergences.label: The finished Mariner arrives at Alfoxden
convergences.note: For Coleridge the end of four months' work; for Dorothy one line before the starlight.

convergences.label: Lyrical Ballads published and judged
convergences.note: Southey condemned the Mariner in print; Lamb defended it in a private letter to him; Coleridge was in Germany and heard of it by post.

convergences.label: Christabel dropped
convergences.note: Dorothy records the verdict flatly after two evenings of delighted readings; Coleridge's letters explain it away.

convergences.label: The second edition reaches its readers
convergences.note: Lamb and John Wordsworth read the same volumes in London in the same week: one argued with the Preface, the other worried that the praise was too obviously from friends.

convergences.label: April 1802: Dejection and daffodils
convergences.note: Within seventeen days Coleridge wrote his lament to Sara, Dorothy saw the daffodils, and Coleridge recited the lament in the cottage — the most crowded fortnight of the journal.

convergences.label: Westminster Bridge, Calais, Scafell
convergences.note: The same few days hold Dorothy's prose and William's sonnet on the same dawn view, the meeting with Annette and Caroline that Dorothy describes almost only as landscape, and Coleridge alone on the fells writing to Sara.

convergences.label: The wedding day
convergences.note: Dorothy's entry is the only intimate record of the day; Coleridge's 'Dejection' appeared in print the same morning. Neither writer comments on the other.

ties.note: Brother and sister; she copied, recited and supplied the observed material for many of his poems.
Daily companions at Alfoxden; at Grasmere Coleridge's arrivals and departures are among her most emotional entries.
Joint authors of Lyrical Ballads; who shaped whom is argued both ways by critics and was argued by the poets themselves.
The government agent named Poole's circle as the local centre of democrats.
Neighbour, patron and closest correspondent through the German winter.
Publisher of the 1798 Lyrical Ballads; sold the edition on to London without Wordsworth's knowledge.
Heard him preach in January 1798 and stayed three weeks at Stowey in spring 1798.
Lamb answered Southey's review of the Mariner in a private letter of November 1798.
The 1801 exchange over the second edition and the Preface.
Married to sisters; Southey took over Greta Hall and supported Coleridge's family.
Brother; read and judged the 1800 poems; his death in 1805 is the chapter's coda.
Mother of his daughter Caroline; met again at Calais in August 1802.
Fan of the poems from 1803; later lived in Dove Cottage and wrote the best-known outside portrait of Dorothy.
She recorded his verses to Sara on 21 April 1802 and was distressed by them.

threads_out.note: Wordsworth lived in revolutionary France in 1791–92, where Annette Vallon bore their daughter Caroline at Orléans; the war that began in February 1793 kept them apart until the Peace of Amiens allowed the Calais meeting of August 1802.

Wordsworth asked Cottle in 1798 for Erasmus Darwin's Zoonomia and drew 'Goody Blake and Harry Gill' from a case in it; Coleridge had met Erasmus Darwin, Charles Darwin's grandfather, at Derby in 1796.

Coleridge's mathematics master at Christ's Hospital was William Wales, who observed the 1769 transit of Venus at Hudson Bay and sailed with Cook; scholars since John Livingston Lowes have traced the Ancient Mariner's seascapes partly to the voyage literature Wales knew.
Wales sailed as astronomer on Cook's second voyage, the one that followed the Endeavour; Cook's accounts were among the voyage books that fed the Ancient Mariner's southern ocean.
